issue: Can a district court consider an intervening First Step Act sentencing change that Congress made expressly nonretroactive (here, the § 924(c) stacking amendment) when deciding whether extraordinary and compelling reasons support compassionate release?

sides.position: Such nonretroactive sentencing statutes may neither support nor contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.
cases: United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582, 586 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255, 261 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Thacker, 4 F.4th 569, 574 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1185 (D.C. Cir. 2022)

sides.position: Such nonretroactive sentencing statutes may be considered in connection with other factors when assessing extraordinary and compelling reasons.
cases: United States v. Ruvalcaba, 26 F.4th 14 (1st Cir. 2022)
United States v. McCoy, 981 F.3d 271 (4th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Chen, No. 20-50333, 2022 WL 4231313 (9th Cir. Sept. 14, 2022)
United States v. McGee, 992 F.3d 1035, 1047–48 (10th Cir. 2021)

this_court: Adopts the Third, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits' position: nonretroactive sentencing statutes may not support a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons.
quote: The circuits have split on whether courts may consider such intervening but expressly nonretroactive sentencing statutes.
cite: United States v. Curtis Jenkins, 50 F.4th 1185 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
